narrative:
The model estimates an 18% chance that you will fail your final year. That does not mean failure is certain; it means about one in five similar students did not pass, and in this process that risk is treated as serious enough to require remedial courses as a precaution.

The strongest factor in the model’s view was your past record: you have no previous class failures, and this was the most important signal, pulling you toward passing. The second most important was your intention to continue into higher education, which you said yes to; that also pulled you toward passing. The third was not having attended nursery school, which the model treated as a slight protective factor, also pulling toward passing. So the top signals are mostly strengths, not warning signs.

That leaves the 18% risk coming from smaller combined patterns. One useful comparison is attendance: you have six absences, compared with an average of about four among students who passed. Your study time of two to five hours a week is common but not high. To improve, focus on consistent attendance, increase weekly study toward five to ten hours where possible, use the family support you already have, and ask for help early if a subject starts to slip.
